e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “jump for joy”: it describes expressing intense gladness with lively, outward rejoicing. The word presents joy as active and overflowing rather than merely quiet or inward. It occurs 68 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, especially in Psalms, where it commonly expresses exuberant rejoicing. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a vigorous expression of great joy.

This word is the personal name “Adam,” also rendered “Atham.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 31 times, with most occurrences in Genesis and additional occurrences in Sirach, 1 Chronicles, and Deuteronomy. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 2:16, and its use continues through Sirach 49:16, showing that the name remains a recognized biblical designation across these writings.

Athaia is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name is rendered “Athaia” and is also given as “Athea.” In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 11:4. Because this word functions as a personal name, its meaning is chiefly identification: it tells the reader who is being named, rather than describing that person’s character or role. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “unequipped,” describing something that lacks what is needed to be ready for a task or purpose. It expresses a condition of being without the necessary equipment or provision rather than an action performed by someone. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it appears once, in Genesis 1:2. As a word-level meaning, it identifies a state or condition; the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text.

This verb means “rub.” It describes the action of rubbing something, whether by moving one thing against another or applying something through rubbing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times across 17 verses, so it represents a repeated action rather than a title, object, or abstract idea. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being rubbed and the surrounding sentence. The word appears from Genesis through Micah in the LXX corpus.

This Greek LXX verb means to spread out or unfold. It describes an action in which something is opened, extended, or made to lie outward rather than remaining closed or gathered. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Job 39:26. Its basic sense is therefore clear, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being spread or unfolded in that passage.

Anar is a personal name, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 6:55, and is presented as “Anar.” Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s precise identity and role in that genealogy cannot be explained further. Its meaning is therefore best represented as the proper name Anar itself.

This word means “cave,” referring to a natural hollow or chamber in rock or the earth. It is a noun naming a place rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 16:18. The word itself gives the basic meaning of the location, while the surrounding verse determines how that cave functions in the passage. Its occurrence is preserved in the Greek Old Testament corpus and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament word.

This verb means “pierce through”: to drive or pass through something by piercing it. It describes a penetrating action rather than a general touch or strike. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, so its basic sense remains consistent while its precise force depends on what is being pierced and the surrounding sentence. The word presents piercing as an action that goes through an object or person, not merely toward it.

This verb means “respond”: it describes giving a reply to what someone has said or asked. It presents speech as a reaction within a conversation, whether the reply is directed to a person or answers a matter being raised. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 242 times, showing that responding is a regular part of recorded dialogue. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This noun means a “plea alleged in defence”—a statement or appeal offered to answer an accusation or defend oneself. It presents a defence rather than simply naming an accusation. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Jeremiah 20:12. That single occurrence identifies its normal lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific force of the word in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “plow”: to break and prepare soil for planting. It describes an ordinary farming action and can be used wherever Scripture speaks about working fields, animals used for cultivation, or the results of agricultural labor. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, with occurrences from Deuteronomy through Sirach. As a verb, it expresses the action itself rather than the field, tool, or person doing the work.

Asēl, also rendered Asil, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a descriptive word, so its meaning is primarily identification. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 1 Chronicles 8:39 and once in Ezekiel 27:19. Without the surrounding verse text, the evidence identifies the name and its locations but does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity.

This Greek LXX verb means “have full view,” describing the act of seeing something with a complete or direct view. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs four times in the LXX corpus: once in Jonah and three times in the deuterocanonical books, including 3 and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes a voice or sound that is deep in tone. It focuses on the quality of the sound, rather than identifying the speaker or explaining the message being spoken. In ordinary English, “deep-voiced” can describe a person, an utterance, or another sound with a low, resonant character. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:48. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and verse context.

This adverb means “firmly” and “steadly,” describing an action done with firmness, certainty, or steadiness. It tells how something is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Leviticus 25:30 and once in 3 Maccabees 5:42. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains doing something firmly or steadily.

This word is a proper name for a place, rendered as “Bēthzaith” or “Vithzeth.” It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but identifies a specific location. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Maccabees 7:19. The available information establishes its identity as a place name, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the location’s particular role in that passage.

This word means “butter,” the nourishing food made from milk or cream. It is a noun used for a physical provision or rich food, appearing nine times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus. Its references span passages from Genesis through Isaiah, where butter is mentioned among foods, provisions, or signs of abundance. The word itself identifies the food plainly; the surrounding verse determines whether it is being offered, enjoyed, stored, or used in a broader picture of plenty.

Gadarathi, also rendered Gatharathi, is a proper name identifying a person or people associated with that name. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a specific designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:5. The supplied information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the individual’s role or significance in that passage.

This adjective describes something marked by grief, sorrow, or lament: “mournful” or “lamentable.” It can characterize a sound, condition, expression, or situation that calls forth mourning. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:25. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise thing it describes in that passage must be understood from the verse’s context, but its basic sense remains sorrowful and suited to lament.

Dabri is a personal name, rendered “Dabri” and also identified as “Thavri.” As a proper name, it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Leviticus 24:11. The name’s precise significance or any connection to the person must come from the surrounding passage, which is not represented here.

Dennaba, also given as Thennava, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. The name occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Genesis 36:32, 1 Chronicles 1:43, and Job 42:17. Its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage.

Demetrios, also rendered Thimitrios, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In this Greek LXX corpus, the name occurs 46 times across 45 verses, appearing in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its reference to the individual called Demetrios; the surrounding passage is needed to identify which person is intended in a particular occurrence.

This adjective describes something as “two cubits long” or “broad.” It gives a measurement or indicates considerable width, rather than naming an object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Numbers 11:31. The word’s basic force is therefore a physical description of size: something extends to the length of two cubits or is broad in proportion. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which aspect is emphasized there.

This Greek LXX adjective means “double” or “twice,” describing something that has two parts, twice the amount, or a twofold measure. It can therefore refer either to a doubled thing or to an action or amount occurring two times. The word appears 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic sense is consistent across a range of passages. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what object, amount, or action it describes.

This adjective describes something that is difficult to explain or put into words. It conveys the idea of being hard to describe, without by itself stating why the subject is difficult to express. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:1. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the word’s normal meaning identifies the difficulty of description rather than supplying the full context.

ἑδράζω is a verb meaning “fixed”: it describes setting something firmly in place or making it established. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, so its basic idea is clear, though its exact force depends on what is being fixed. It appears once each in Proverbs, Wisdom, and Sirach. The word points to firmness, stability, or settled placement rather than temporary movement.

This Greek LXX verb means “narrate out”: to tell or recount something in a full, developed way. It describes the act of expressing events, matters, or experiences through an account rather than merely mentioning them. The wording presents narration as something brought out clearly for others to hear or understand. It occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “suck the breast,” describing an infant nursing at the breast. It names the physical act of receiving milk in this way, rather than a general idea of eating or drinking. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 66:11. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself refers specifically to breastfeeding or nursing. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Old Testament translation corpus.

Elibamas is a proper name, also rendered Elivamas. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 1:52. Because the available passage information does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the name itself can be explained only as this personal designation, without assigning it an additional meaning or significance.

This Greek LXX adjective means “ninth,” describing something that comes after eight others in sequence or marks the ninth position in a series. It can identify a day, month, date, or other counted place, depending on the sentence where it appears. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, consistently referring to the ninth position or time. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun means “direction; injunction”: an instruction or command that tells someone what is required or expected. It commonly refers to an authoritative directive, whether given as a rule to follow or as guidance for conduct. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 222 times, showing that this is a well-established term for binding instruction rather than a casual suggestion.

This Greek LXX verb means “increase”: to become greater or to make something greater. It expresses growth or expansion rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:25. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise role in that sentence must be determined from the passage itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “invoke” or “nickname”: it can express calling upon someone or giving someone a name. Its central idea is an act of calling, whether directed toward a person or expressed in assigning a name. The word occurs 173 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears. It is found from Genesis through 4 Maccabees, showing that this basic idea is used across many kinds of biblical writing.

This Greek LXX verb means “turn over” or “permit.” It describes giving someone or something into another person’s control, or allowing an action to take place. As a verb, it expresses an act of handing over, granting permission, or allowing circumstances to proceed. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, so its exact force depends on what is being handed over or permitted in each passage.

This noun means “worked; arable,” describing land that has been cultivated or is suitable for cultivation. It refers to ground understood in relation to farming or productive use, rather than simply naming land in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 20:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s central idea is farmland that can be worked.

gl: easily handled; easy to deal with
d: easily handled; easy to deal with

e.t: This adjective describes something that is easily handled or easy to deal with. It can refer to a matter, task, or situation that does not present much difficulty. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains manageability—something a person can take up, work with, or address without unusual trouble.

Zare is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Zare” and does not function as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader meaning. The name appears six times in six verses, across Genesis, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Job. Because the available material identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its particular family or historical association must be understood from each passage. This LXX name should remain distinct from similarly rendered names in other biblical language collections.

“Sweet-voiced” describes a voice or sound that is pleasant and pleasing to hear. As an adjective, the word characterizes the quality of someone’s voice rather than naming an action or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 33:32. That single occurrence identifies its normal lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the description functions there. The word therefore points to vocal attractiveness or a pleasant sound.

This Greek LXX verb means “nurse”: to feed a child from the breast and care for the child in that nourishing role. It describes an action, so it may refer to a woman nursing an infant, but its central idea is giving nourishment through breastfeeding. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages connected with infants, children, and nurturing care. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Iabok, also rendered Iavok, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. The name occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Judges, including references in Genesis 32, Numbers 21, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Judges. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and setting, but the word itself functions as a place name. The alternate renderings preserve the same name in English.

Iath is a proper name, preserved as “Iath” rather than translated into a descriptive meaning. As a name, it identifies a particular person or entity named Iath in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 24:22. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain anything more about the individual or the name’s role there.

This adjective describes someone as having a pious soul—an inner life devoted to reverence for God. It points to a person's spiritual character rather than naming an outward action or object. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, in 4 Maccabees 17:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a person marked by inward godly devotion.

This noun means “horse,” referring to the animal used for riding, transport, work, or warfare. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 188 times, including references to individual horses and groups of horses. The word appears across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic meaning remains consistent whether the surrounding passage concerns travel, armies, kings, or ordinary activity. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Iōbel is a proper name identifying a person, rendered in the Greek Old Testament as “Iōbel” or “Iovel.” It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its main function is personal identification. This LXX form occurs once, in Genesis 4:20. The name’s specific significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

Καδες is a proper name rendered “Kades” or “Kathes.” It identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Joshua: once in Joshua 19:37 and once in Joshua 21:32. Without the surrounding verse text, the precise referent cannot be identified more narrowly, but the word’s basic function is a proper name preserved in these two passages.

This Greek LXX noun means “palm frond,” the leafy branch or segment of a palm tree. It names a physical plant part rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 23:40. The exact significance of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: a frond taken from a palm tree.

This word means “and if,” joining an additional condition or possibility to what has already been said. It can connect two parts of a sentence while introducing a circumstance that may or may not occur. As a conjunction, its role is relational rather than naming a person, action, or object. It occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including Leviticus, Wisdom, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Kariōth is a proper name, also rendered Karioth. It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:24. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide a further ordinary meaning or description, so its specific referent must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

gl: stick fast in the ground; plant firmly
d: stick fast in the ground; plant firmly

e.t: This verb means “stick fast in the ground” or “plant firmly.” It describes making something fixed, rooted, or firmly set in place rather than merely placing it loosely. As a verb, it expresses an action: something is established so that it remains secure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in 1 Samuel and Hosea. The surrounding verse determines whether the image is literal or used as a comparison, but the central idea remains firm setting or rooted placement.

This verb means to view something closely or survey it carefully. It describes deliberate inspection rather than a passing glance, often involving examining a place or situation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 26 times, with many uses in Numbers, where careful surveying is prominent. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being inspected and the surrounding sentence.

This word means a bell, a small object that makes a ringing sound. It is a noun used for actual bells associated with priestly clothing and with decorative or sacred furnishings. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, mainly in Exodus, with further occurrences in 2 Chronicles and Sirach. Its basic meaning remains concrete: it identifies the bell itself rather than an action, sound, or symbolic quality. The surrounding verse determines its particular use.

This adjective means “hewn,” describing something cut or shaped from a harder material, such as stone or wood. It points to an object formed by deliberate physical work rather than something left in its natural state. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Deuteronomy 4:49. Its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse text, but the word itself emphasizes the shaped or cut condition of the thing described.

This noun means a “fattening substance,” referring to something used to enrich or increase the nourishing quality of food. Its meaning is specific rather than broad: it names a substance associated with making food richer. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Nehemiah 8:10. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly how the word functions there, but its basic sense remains a fattening or enriching food substance.

Maththanai is a proper name, also rendered “Maththane.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:19. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the available information does not establish anything further about the person’s role or significance. The name’s normal meaning in this corpus is therefore simply the personal designation Maththanai or Maththane.

Maisalōth, also rendered Mesaloth, is a proper name. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Maccabees 9:2. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s specific referent cannot be described further without adding information beyond the lexical meaning.

Matthan is a proper name referring to a person named Matthan. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice: once in 2 Kings 11:18 and once in 2 Chronicles 23:17. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name itself does not establish further details about Matthan’s identity, character, role, or actions. Its meaning at the lexical level is simply the personal name “Matthan,” rather than a general word describing an object, quality, action, or relationship.

This Greek LXX particle means “first of all.” It marks something as coming first in an ordering of thoughts, statements, or matters. Rather than naming a person, object, or action, it helps organize what is being said and signals an initial point. The word occurs 215 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, so its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “anxiety”—the troubled concern or worry that weighs on a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 11 times, showing that it names a recognizable inner burden rather than an action or object. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding words and situation, but the central idea remains anxious concern. The word occurs across books including Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Daniel, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees.

This Greek LXX verb means to “associate” with something or to “partake of” it. It describes sharing in, taking part in, or having a connection with something rather than merely observing it. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Proverbs, Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what the person or thing is joining, sharing, or receiving.

This noun refers to a “mention” or “remembrance”—bringing someone or something to mind in speech or thought. It can name the act of mentioning as well as the resulting remembrance. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs 14 times, showing that it is used across several books rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Myrsinōn is a proper name, preserved as “Myrsinōn” or “Mirsinon” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in Judges 1:35. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain whether it refers to a person, place, or other named subject; that requires the actual verse and its surrounding context.

This word refers to “sheep breeders,” people whose work involves raising and caring for sheep. It is a noun naming a particular kind of livestock worker rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 1:1. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its specific role in that sentence must be understood from that context.

Nasoue, also rendered Nasue, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:54. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular person or family rather than a concept to define. The available biblical record does not provide a broader lexical sense or additional occurrences for comparison.

This noun means “entertainment,” referring to something that provides enjoyment or amusement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 15:17. Because the word appears only once and the verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains a form of pleasure or diversion, expressed as something enjoyable rather than as an action word.

This verb means “slip and fall” or simply “slip.” It describes losing stable footing and falling, or the act of slipping itself. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In this Greek corpus, it occurs eight times, appearing once in Proverbs and seven times in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective means “whole” or “wholly,” describing something complete, entire, or undivided. It can characterize a person or thing as complete in extent, or describe an action carried out fully. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 242 times, showing broad use for completeness rather than a narrow or specialized idea. Its exact sense depends on the noun or action it describes, but the central thought remains entirety: nothing is left out or held back.

This Greek LXX preposition means “about” or “around.” It describes something as concerning a subject or located near and surrounding something else. Its precise sense depends on the words and situation in the sentence, but the central idea is relation to a surrounding subject, place, or matter. It is widely used across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, occurring 766 times in this LXX corpus.

This adjective describes something covered with gold or made to appear gold-plated. It refers to an outer layer or finish of gold rather than necessarily describing something made entirely of solid gold. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs seven times, all in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the object being described, but its central meaning remains a gold-covered or gilded appearance.

e.h: A Curl or Lock of Hair
e.t: This noun refers to a curl or a lock of hair. It names a distinct coil or gathered strand rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Song of Songs 7:6. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is simply a curl or lock of hair.

This adjective describes someone or something marked by “with many tears,” emphasizing an abundance of tears rather than merely the presence of one tear. It describes a tearful condition or appearance, while the surrounding sentence determines the specific situation or emotion involved. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 5:25. The word’s basic sense remains focused on the visible presence of many tears.

This adjective describes something that projects outward or hangs over, especially with a steep, looming shape. It means “beetling” or “overhanging,” drawing attention to the physical position or appearance of an object rather than to an action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 7:5. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word is a proper name rendered “Reēma” or “Rhima.” It identifies a named individual or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not specify which. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Genesis 22:24. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its precise reference in that passage cannot be described further. The central meaning is therefore the name itself: Reema or Rhima.

Saba, also written Sava, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named person or place according to its surrounding passage, but the name itself does not carry a broader definition. It occurs 20 times across 18 verses, from Genesis through Ezekiel. The English rendering is usually “Saba.”

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named Samer, also given as Samir. It is not a common noun describing an action, quality, or object, but an individual’s name in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in 1 Chronicles. Its exact reference is recorded in 1 Chronicles 7:32 and 24:24, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each person’s place in those passages.

This word means “sandal,” the footwear worn on the foot. It is a noun referring to a simple item of clothing or travel equipment. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Joshua and once in Isaiah, showing that its basic meaning remains concrete and consistent across its uses. The precise significance of a sandal in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but the word itself names the footwear rather than an action, quality, or person.

Sarathi is a proper name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its recorded meaning is simply “Sarathi”; no additional lexical definition is provided. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:2. Because it is a personal name, its significance comes from the person and surrounding genealogy in that passage, not from a broader dictionary sense of the name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “rot”: to undergo decay, spoil, or physical breakdown. It describes something losing its soundness rather than remaining whole and healthy. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented here, including passages from Job, Psalms, Ezekiel, Sirach, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is described as decaying, but its central idea remains deterioration or corruption over time.

This noun means “shelter” or “protection”: a covering or safe defense that guards someone from harm. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 33:27. The word’s basic sense points to protective care rather than merely a physical structure, though the surrounding verse determines how that protection is expressed there. Its meaning is therefore concise and focused: something that shelters, covers, or keeps safe.

This verb means “look carefully for.” It describes an intentional search in which someone gives focused attention rather than glancing casually. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Old Testament books and once in Bel and the Dragon. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea remains attentive seeking or inspection. The word is represented in Genesis, Exodus, Zechariah, and Bel and the Dragon.

This noun means “cave,” referring to a natural hollow or enclosed place in the ground or rock. It is used for physical locations in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including places where people may enter, hide, dwell, or bury the dead. The word occurs 52 times in this LXX corpus, so its basic meaning is broad and consistent rather than limited to one particular setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “pillar”: an upright structure that supports or stands as a vertical post. It is used for architectural features such as supports in the tabernacle and other buildings. The word occurs 146 times in the Greek LXX, with many uses in Exodus and other Old Testament books. Its central idea remains a substantial upright support, whether referring to a single post or multiple pillars. The exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description.
